Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================  
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD).

Rationale  
• Treatment is assigned deterministically by whether a one-dimensional score (Democratic vote-share margin at t-1) crosses a known cutoff (0).  
• Close elections generate as-good-as-random assignment because campaigns cannot perfectly manipulate the realized vote share at the single-percentage-point level.  
• The RDD therefore isolates ex-ante identical districts that differ only in the party that becomes incumbent, allowing credible estimation of the causal “incumbency advantage.”  
• The same logic underlies dozens of economic applications with administrative thresholds; hence a well-specified RDD serves as a template for the broader “user guide.”

----------------------------------------------------------------  
## 2. Treatment and Control  

Running variable:  
m_it = Democratic two-party vote share in district i at election t-1 minus 0.50 (so m_it = 0 at a 50% share).

Cutoff: m_it = 0.  

Treatment indicator (T_i):  
T_i = 1{m_it ≥ 0}. A district is “treated” if the Democrat barely wins at t-1 and therefore enters election t as the incumbent party.

Control group:  
Districts with −h < m_it < 0 (barely lost).  

Outcome variables (Y_it):  
1. Democratic vote share at t.  
2. Indicator = 1 if Democrat wins at t.  
(Timing: treatment occurs between elections t-1 and t.)

----------------------------------------------------------------  
## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Continuity of potential outcomes:  
E[Y_i(1) | m_i = c] and E[Y_i(0) | m_i = c] are continuous in m_i at c = 0.  
Plausibility: Individual votes are noisy; small differences in aggregate share are effectively random.  

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable:  
Actors cannot sort exactly above/below the 50% line.  
Plausibility: Candidates cannot perfectly forecast turnout or every voter’s choice. Empirically testable via McCrary density.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers):  
The treatment status of one district does not affect another’s outcome near the cutoff.  
Plausibility: Elections are largely district-specific; any statewide or national spillovers are smooth in m_i.  

A4. Local ignorability of covariates:  
Pretreatment covariates are balanced at the cutoff.  
Plausibility: Follows from A1; check via balance tests.  

A5. Correct functional form and bandwidth choice:  
Local linear fits within optimally chosen bandwidths recover the limit from both sides.  
Address with data-driven bandwidths and robustness to alternatives.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
## 4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

T1. Sorting / Manipulation around the cutoff  
• Test density with McCrary (rdrobust::rddensity).  
• Inspect bunching plots.  
• If evidence of sorting: restrict to tighter bandwidths where manipulation is implausible; employ local randomization methods (rdrandinf).  

T2. Functional-form misspecification / bandwidth sensitivity  
• Use local linear and local quadratic specifications.  
• Report estimates across Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik (CCT) MSE-optimal, half- and double-bandwidths.  

T3. Heterogeneous treatment effects limiting external validity  
• Present subgroup analyses (e.g., South vs. non-South, era pre-/post-1964).  
• Emphasize that estimates identify the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) for close races, cautioning about extrapolation to safe districts.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# --- 0. Libraries ------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)      # main RD estimation
library(rddensity)     # McCrary test
library(fixest)        # alternative parametric checks

# --- 1. Load Data ------------------------------------------------------------
# Assume 'lee2008.csv' has district-year observations
df <- read_csv("lee2008.csv")   # district, year, dem_share_tminus1, dem_share_t

# --- 2. Variable Construction -----------------------------------------------
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(
    margin_tm1 = dem_share_tminus1 - 0.5,   # running variable centered at 0
    treat      = if_else(margin_tm1 >= 0, 1, 0),
    outcome_vs = dem_share_t,               # vote share at t
    outcome_win = if_else(dem_share_t >= 0.5, 1, 0)
  )

# --- 3. Main RD Estimation ---------------------------------------------------
# Democratic vote share as outcome
rd_vs  <- rdrobust(y = df$outcome_vs, x = df$margin_tm1)
summary(rd_vs)

# Democratic win indicator as outcome
rd_win <- rdrobust(y = df$outcome_win, x = df$margin_tm1)
summary(rd_win)

# --- 4. Density Test ---------------------------------------------------------
dens <- rddensity(df$margin_tm1)
summary(dens)
plot(dens)

# --- 5. Covariate Balance Check (example: lagged turnout) --------------------
rd_cov <- rdrobust(y = df$turnout_tm1, x = df$margin_tm1)
summary(rd_cov)

# --- 6. Robustness: Half & Double Bandwidths ---------------------------------
rd_vs_half   <- rdrobust(y=df$outcome_vs, x=df$margin_tm1, h=rd_vs$bws[1]/2)
rd_vs_double <- rdrobust(y=df$outcome_vs, x=df$margin_tm1, h=rd_vs$bws[1]*2)

# --- 7. Alternative Parametric Spec (global poly) ----------------------------
df_subset <- df %>% filter(abs(margin_tm1) < 0.10)   # ±10pp window
lm_poly <- feols(outcome_vs ~ treat + poly(margin_tm1,3,raw=TRUE), data=df_subset)
summary(lm_poly)
```

----------------------------------------------------------------  
## 6. Expected Results  

Economic theory on incumbency predicts a positive effect: having the seat allows resource advantages, name recognition, and constituent services. Prior literature (Lee 2008) finds ≈6–8 percentage-point higher vote share and ≈6–10 p.p. higher win probability for barely Democratic incumbents relative to barely non-incumbents. I therefore expect:  
• Δ Vote share ≈ +7 p.p. (0.07) at the cutoff.  
• Δ Win probability ≈ +0.08.

----------------------------------------------------------------  
## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Sharp RDD)  

C1: No manipulation of running variable at cutoff ………………… 1  
C2: Covariate continuity/balance at cutoff ………………………………… 1  
C3: Robustness to varying bandwidths & functional forms ………… 1  
C4: Placebo/false cutoff tests show no discontinuity elsewhere … 0.5 (need to implement)  
C5: External validity explicitly discussed & subgroup heterogeneity analyzed … 0.5  

Total (out of 5) = 4.0  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
This plan delivers a transparent, replicable template for assessing threshold-based causal claims across economic applications while demonstrating implementation in the canonical U.S. House election setting.
